newsitem.title: BURMA: FEATURE - Ancient ruins of Pagan awe Burma visitors.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ancient ruins of Pagan awe Burma visitors.

text.p: It used to be called the City of Four Million Pagodas.
Although the ancient Burmese capital of Pagan may no longer glitter as it did 900 years ago, it is still one of the most inspiring sights in the world.

More than 2,200 temples, stupas and monasteries -- many built in the 11th century during the First Burmese Empire of warrior King Anawrahta -- are still scattered across the dusty landcape in various states of repair.

On the drive into the Pagan Archaeological Zone in central Burma, a visitor sees one ruin after another. Some were built nearly on top of each other, stretching in the brick-red dirt into the horizon.
Elegant, gilded temples stand next to crumbled ruins of stupas or icons, which are being restored.

There are also nearly 300 mounds of ruins that have not yet been excavated for financial reasons and because most of the archeologists' time has been spent organising restoration of some of the largest and most unstable temples and ruins.
"There are some temples we need to repair urgently," says Aung Kyaing, director of Pagan's Department of Archaeology.

Although Pagan's dry, arid climate has helped preserve a lot of the old buildings, Aung Kyaing said many temples suffered serious damage during a major earthquake in 1975. Before the earthquake there were about 4,500 ruins in decent condition.
RECONSTRUCTION CAUSES CONTROVERSY
The reconstruction has caused controversy both in and outside Burma, partly because of the way it has been done, and for the lives it has disrupted.
"I admit some people don't like what we're doing," said Aung Kyaing, who said UNESCO had donated about $17.3 million to help restore ruins in the ancient religious capital of Burma.
"But we are training local people to restore the ruins in the original style," he said.
But some of the ruins in the process of being restored look out of place as new terracotta tops are put on stupas that have a base of ancient, uncemented bricks.
It is virtually impossible to replicate some of the previous building styles like the mortarless brickwork and intricate terracing that took years to complete.

Legend has it that former King Narathu was so demanding in building the Dhammayangyi Temple, one of the more famous pagodas, that he ordered the masons' heads chopped off if he discovered a pin could fit between any two bricks.
BURMA ACCUSED OF ABUSES

Some international human rights organisations have accused Burma's military government of using forced labour to restore the Pagan ruins so they could be ready in time for the official tourism year that began last November.

The government in 1990 also relocated the entire walled city of Old Pagan, which was right in the middle of the Archaeological Zone on the banks of the Irrawaddy River, to a peanut plantation several kilometres away.

The village of about 2,000 people -- formerly the area's tourism centre -- was forced to move in only a few days. The government later cleared the guesthouses of Old Pagan, refurbished a few hotels within the Archaeological Zone and built new hotels in nearby towns.
The government says it was a necessary change in order to preserve the ruins and one of the nation's most valuable assets.
"Inside the city's walls we kept finding many sites we needed to excavate. They were getting ruined because of all the people, so we had to remove them," Aung Kyaing said.
A lacquerware salesman at the Ananda Temple said he still resents the government having forced his family to move away from Old Pagan.
"I now have to go seven miles to get to work," he said. "On my bicycle, that can take a long time. Before it was really close and I could go to my shop and home easily. Not now."

Now the former thriving tourist hub of Old Pagan is more like a ghost-town. Near dusk, virtually the only sound is the "clop, clop" of horse hooves as horse-cart drivers bring tourists to the temples to watch the sun set over the ruins.
